questions.title: How can a court fairly rule on a FOIA request based on ex parte declarations?
questions.question_body: I'm confused by the court's reliance on 'ex parte' declarations in Section V. Since the purpose of the Freedom of Information Act is transparency, doesn't allowing the government to submit secret evidence to the court—without the plaintiff seeing it—undermine the very essence of the law? How can a plaintiff effectively challenge a finding of 'non-segregability' if the justification for that finding is kept secret?

questions.title: What is the specific threshold for an investigation to be considered 'reasonably anticipated' under Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: The court notes that 'ongoing criminal investigations' count as 'proceedings' and that the government may show this simply by attesting to their 'existence.' Does this mean that as long as an agent says they are 'looking into' something, the records are automatically exempt? At what point does a 'potential' investigation become 'reasonably anticipated' enough to trigger Exemption 7(A)?

questions.title: How much 'deference' should the court actually give the FBI regarding national security concerns?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that because the FBI specializes in law enforcement, its decisions are 'entitled to deference,' particularly regarding counterterrorism. Does this 'deference' mean the court is essentially rubber-stamping the FBI's claims? If the FBI asserts a national security risk, what is the actual standard of review for the court to determine if that claim is factually true or just a convenient way to withhold records?

questions.title: What distinguishes 'reasonably segregable' information from information that is 'inextricably intertwined'?
questions.question_body: I'm struggling with the distinction made in Section V regarding 'line-by-line' redactions. The court says that if non-exempt material is randomly interspersed, it isn't 'reasonably segregable.' Does this imply that the government can avoid the burden of precise redaction by simply claiming a document is too cluttered? How does the court define the boundary between 'meaningful information' and 'words'?

questions.title: What specific evidence is required to establish a 'nexus' between a subject and a law enforcement duty?
questions.question_body: Section IV.A mentions that the FBI must establish a 'rational nexus between the investigation and one of the agency's law enforcement duties.' In this case, the court seemed to accept Farahi's connections to known terrorists as sufficient. Does the government have to prove that a specific crime is being actively planned, or is the mere fact that a person is 'associated' with a security risk enough to establish a nexus?
